input_parts.part1:
You go to buy your usual coffee, then stop. “Hey, when did you go upscale?” The first thing that comes to mind is tariffs. You want to say, “So you’re the culprit!” But a great detective takes a breath here. Let’s turn back the clock on this case.

In the United States, the average price of ground coffee rose 41% from the same month a year earlier, according to reports based on government figures. This is about ground coffee, not a cup at a café. Before you buy something to wake you up, the price shocks your wallet awake.

But according to Reuters, most of the rise in store prices came from bean shortages that began before the summer tariffs and from higher prices for the beans themselves. Wait a minute. The case had started before the suspect we had our eye on even appeared.
input_parts.part2:
The investigation takes us to Brazil. A drought was happening there. Hopes that the next harvest would recover had also faded. “Will there be enough beans?” Before thinking about how to brew them, the question was whether there would be beans to brew at all.

Turn the pages of the record, and we find that in February, before summer, the futures price for Arabica coffee in New York reached an all-time high. This was not the price of ground coffee in stores, but the market price for trading coffee beans. The market alarm had already sounded.

“So, are tariffs off the hook?” No, that would be jumping to conclusions too. Reuters also reported that the tariffs the United States imposed in summer pushed up the price of the beans themselves. They did play a part. But we must get the order of events right.
input_parts.part3:
The key point is that, at the time of that report, the tariff-driven rise had not yet fully made its way through the supply chain to the prices consumers paid. The moment the cost of the beans goes up, the store price tag does not jump up and say, “Got it!” Price rises take time to show up.

In other words, a price tag is not a live news broadcast. It is a letter that arrives a little late. Even if you open it today, it may not be about something that happened today. It may tell you about an earlier drought or bean shortage, or high prices in the market. If you look only at the latest headline, you may get the sender wrong.

Next time you look twice at a price tag in the store, try adding “When did this happen?” to “Why is it expensive?” Coffee may be bitter, but we want our detective work to be clear. Before that first cup, turn back the hands of the clock a little.

input_parts.part1:
You get on the train. You find a seat. At last, you can relax—or so you think. Then you hear video sounds from somewhere: laughter, sound effects, and very upbeat background music. You’re quietly heading home, but your ears are forced to log in to someone else’s recommendations. You bought a train ticket, but you don’t remember buying a ticket to this show.

One smartphone, and the whole carriage is the audience. That’s a pretty bold show.

Here’s news about this kind of “sound delivery nobody asked for.” On October 19, 2026, the UK announced the start of a nationwide campaign encouraging rail passengers to use headphones.

But don’t rush to think, “In the UK, no headphones means you’re breaking the law!” No new rule has been made to ban all sound. The main focus is existing rail rules and a campaign asking people to think of those around them.
input_parts.part2:
The existing rules ban making noise from a device in a way that bothers other people. A smartphone speaker can also be covered, if the situation meets the rules. There is an exception if the rail company has given written permission. A song that’s a masterpiece to you may not sound that way to the person beside you.

If you don’t follow the rules, you could face a fine of up to £1,000. That’s enough to make you reach for your wallet before the volume button. But the key words are “up to” and “could.” It doesn’t mean everyone who plays something through a speaker automatically gets a £1,000 bill.

So the first step is a call to use headphones. The message is due to be shared through posters and announcements at stations and on trains. The fine may be what people hear loudest, but let’s listen to the campaign’s message, too.
input_parts.part3:
Its name is roughly, “Share the journey, not the noise.” Just because we’re in the same carriage doesn’t mean we’ve joined the fan club for the same video. The words draw that line simply.

This isn’t saying, “Don’t enjoy yourself.” It’s more like saying, “Choose who hears the sound.” You can enjoy videos and music. Just don’t make the people around you sit in the audience without asking them. Headphones don’t take away your entertainment. They’re a small screen that keeps the fun in your own seat.

The next time you press play, take a breath. “Who am I sending this sound to?” We’re on the same train, going in the same direction. Still, there’s no need for the sound to ride along into everyone’s ears.

input_segments.y_closing: A missed-delivery notice was left at the home of someone who had chosen a morning time slot, too. For people who can choose how to receive packages, a redelivery fee can be a signal that encourages them to make an effort. But having the person receiving the package pay won’t change late deliveries or how arrival times are shared. The person receiving the package can’t change how much shipping costs or how much of it goes to the people who deliver the packages, either. When you couldn’t be home and had a problem, could you choose how to receive your package? Did you know when it would arrive? Is that a problem that can be changed by charging the person receiving the package?
input_segments.y_intro_1: First to speak is a delivery driver who visits homes every day and delivers packages.
input_segments.y_intro_2: Next is someone who receives packages and is often away from home because both she and her husband work.
input_segments.y_intro_3: Lastly, a person who chooses to pick up packages at a locker or another place and takes steps to avoid redelivery.
input_segments.y_lead: What if it cost money to have a package delivered again when you were not home at the time it arrived? Charging for redelivery means the person receiving the package pays a fee on top of the usual shipping cost. How should we decide whether to charge a fee or reduce redeliveries in another way? Let’s hear from three people with different lives and points of view.
input_segments.y_voice_1: When I leave a notice saying nobody was home and head off, I feel a little down, too. But then I go to the next house. I really would like to see fewer redeliveries, and they are hard on us, too. Even so, I can’t just say that customers should pay the cost. I think it makes more sense to cover the cost through the overall fee for carrying packages than to charge each customer who wasn’t home for the cost of that redelivery. To do that, I want the company to think about whether free shipping for online orders should stay as it is. If they review shipping fees, I want them to review how the fees are set, too, so that the money really reaches the people who deliver the packages.
input_segments.y_voice_2: Having to pay for redelivery just doesn’t sit right with me. My husband and I are both away at work, so for packages where we can choose a delivery time, we choose a day and time when we know we’ll be home. But once, I chose a morning time slot and the package didn’t come. I went out to take care of an errand, and when I got back, there was a missed-delivery notice. There are also many packages where you can’t choose a time, and you don’t know beforehand when they’ll arrive. Before charging us, I want them to first do something about arriving at the time we chose and telling us when the package will arrive. The delivery workers must have a hard time because there aren’t enough of them, and I guess it can’t be helped. But I can’t accept having to pay for that. Am I wrong to feel this way?
input_segments.y_voice_3: I try to pick up packages at a delivery office or locker so I don’t cause trouble with redelivery. It’s convenient to pick them up when it suits me, but for some items, I can’t choose a locker. And even when I ask for a package to be sent to a delivery office, it may arrive late, so I sometimes end up receiving it in person after all. Still, I take the trouble to think about how to receive my packages, so honestly, I think it’s wrong that I pay the same fee as people who are always away and ask for redelivery. Redelivery takes up the delivery worker’s time, so it’s fine to charge for it. I’d be happy if the first redelivery were free, and people who are repeatedly away had to pay. But maybe that’s just my point of view, since the delivery office is nearby and I can choose how to receive my packages.

input_segments.y_closing: The high school student said that wanting to rely on adults might be “selfish.” The freedom to decide how to use social media and turning to adults when something goes wrong do not fit neatly together. The parent of a middle school child said that even at an age when children are allowed to use it, they won’t suddenly be able to protect themselves. The question of setting an age when children are allowed to use social media also raises the question of how much they can turn to adults after they start. If you let a child in your life use social media, which parts of how they use it would you leave up to them, and what kinds of trouble would you help them with?
input_segments.y_intro_1: First to speak is a parent raising a young child. They think about social media as they watch over their child each day.
input_segments.y_intro_2: Next is a high school student for whom social media is a familiar way to stay in touch with friends. He talks about the issue of children’s use from the user’s side.
input_segments.y_intro_3: Last is a parent who lives with a middle school child. They speak as someone who has to decide at home how their child uses social media.
input_segments.y_lead: If a child tells you they want to use social media, how much should you allow? Restricting how they use it until a certain age is different from banning them from having an account at all. To begin with, should Japan set an age limit on children's use of social media? Let’s hear from three people with different views and lives.
input_segments.y_voice_1: My young child was choosing videos that were too intense and things that could cost money in the app, just because they were interested. When I talk to them, they often say, “Then I won’t do it.” I think they understand when I explain it. But maybe they can’t tell what’s wrong before they choose. I don’t think it’s okay to let them use whatever catches their interest. Seeing that, I feel safer if there are rules for how to use social media based on age. But honestly, when we’re on a long trip and I want them to be quiet, it helps if they watch something, and limits are hard on parents too. Even so, I still can’t say how far I want the rules to go.
input_segments.y_voice_2: I don’t want to be blocked from using social media just because of my age. If even high school students couldn’t have accounts, I think it would be hard to keep in touch with friends. I’m against a ban. I want to have a say in what I can use and how I use it. I want to decide for myself, but I can’t handle everything that happens on my own. If people say bad things about me or threaten me, I’d still want to turn to an adult right away. Maybe that’s selfish of me. Rather than putting the same limits on how everyone can use it based on age, I think there are other things we can do, like setting safety filters. I want the approach to change so it takes our use into account, without even stopping us from keeping in touch with friends.
input_segments.y_voice_3: As a parent raising a middle school child, I want to decide how much to let them use social media based on what they can handle. Rather than drawing the line by age alone, I think it would be better, if possible, for the features they can use to grow step by step as they become able to handle more. I don’t want the choice to be only between letting them use it and banning it. I want to set different stages. If my child started using social media with no preparation the moment they passed the age when it had been banned, that would worry me. I don’t think reaching the age when it’s okay to use it means they’ll suddenly know how to protect themselves. Just as you need to practice swimming before going into the sea, it’s still scary when a child who isn’t ready is suddenly thrown into it.
